RAG in SafeRAG: Benchmarking Security in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Xun Liang, Simin Niu, Zhiyu Li, Sensen Zhang, Hanyu Wang, Feiyu Xiong, Jason Zhaoxin Fan, Bo Tang, Jihao Zhao, Jiawei Yang, Shichao Song, Mengwei Wang · 2025

RAG is an indexing-retrieval-generation paradigm that integrates external, potentially unverified knowledge into large language models to efficiently expand their knowledge boundaries and solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Its pipeline unfolds through retriever, filter, and generator stages: retrieved texts pass through these components before being synthesized into a response. This use of external knowledge also creates attack opportunities. Attackers can inject malicious contexts at any stage and influence final responses, while threats may include noise, conflict, toxicity, DoS, and evasive strategies beyond current evaluations. SafeRAG evaluates RAG security and robustness through retrieval accuracy, retrieval safety, and generation security. The evaluation reveals significant weaknesses in RAG’s retriever, filter, and generator, showing susceptibility to subtle but impactful data-injection threats.

Narrative, section by section

8 sections; each heading opens the text

SafeRAG: Benchmarking Security in Retrieval-Augmented Generation / Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation integrates external knowledge into large language models through an indexing-retrieval-generation paradigm. The text reports that incorporating external and unverified knowledge increases its vulnerability to attacks.

Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation provides an efficient way to expand the knowledge boundaries of large language models through external retrieval. Its retrieved texts pass through multiple components before being synthesized into a response, creating opportunities for attackers to manipulate the process.

Related Work / RAG Security Evaluation Dataset .. RAG Security Evaluation Metric

RAG security evaluation addresses noise, conflict, toxicity, and DoS attacks across the knowledge base, retrieved context, and filtered context. Existing work evaluates RAG using rule-based and model-based methods.

Evaluation Metrics / Retrieval Safety Metric .. Generation Safety Metric / F1 Variant

RAG is evaluated for retrieval accuracy, retrieval safety, and generation security under noise, conflict, toxicity, and DoS attacks.

Conclusion

RAG is shown to have significant weaknesses across its retriever, filter, and generator components. The paper demonstrates that RAG systems are susceptible to subtle yet impactful data injection threats.

Appendix / Potential Risks .. Ethical Considerations

RAG may be exposed to evasive attack strategies that exploit weaknesses beyond the scope of current evaluations. SafeRAG is designed to evaluate and improve RAG security and robustness.

SafeRAG Dataset Construction

Retrieval-augmented generation is the system setting whose security is evaluated using the SafeRAG dataset.

Threat Framework: Attacks on the

The RAG pipeline consists of retrieval, filtering, and generation stages. Attackers may inject malicious contexts into any of these stages to influence the final response.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains

Ran Xu, Hui Liu, Sreyashi Nag, Zhenwei Dai, Yaochen Xie, Xianfeng Tang, Chen Luo, Yang Li, Joyce C. Ho, Carl Yang, Qi He · 2025

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a technique, tool, and question answering system that enhances large language models by integrating external knowledge for knowledge-intensive tasks. It supports question answering, language modeling, long-tail knowledge, and specialized-domain adaptation while avoiding costly retraining and reducing hallucination by grounding outputs in relevant evidence. In its typical approach, a retriever fetches supporting documents or contexts from a large corpus, and a generator or LLM produces answers from that retrieved context. Its development emphasizes dynamic retrieval to refine fetched content, filtering irrelevant contexts for robustness, and instruction fine-tuning to improve search and RAG capabilities. During medical evaluation, it is used at inference with top-10 retrieval results from multiple models; other datasets use top-10 passages fetched through Google Search.

Retrieval-augmented generation enhances the question answering abilities of large language models by integrating external knowledge. General-purpose retrieval-augmented generation systems face challenges when adapted to specialized fields because of distribution shifts and limited domain-specific data.

Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation incorporates external knowledge sources into large language models for knowledge-intensive tasks such as question answering. It can customize responses for long-tail knowledge, avoid costly retraining, and reduce hallucination by grounding outputs in relevant evidence.

Related Work

Retrieval-augmented generation has emerged as a powerful tool for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks such as language modeling and question answering. Recent work improves it through dynamic retrieval, irrelevant-context filtering, and instruction tuning for search and RAG capabilities.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in TableRAG: A Retrieval Augmented Generation Framework for Heterogeneous Document Reasoning

Xiaohan Yu, Pu Jian, Chong Chen · 2025

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a paradigm for open-domain question answering and for mitigating hallucination while improving response reliability. It retrieves relevant document chunks from a knowledge base and incorporates them into generation, commonly by linearizing tables, chunking them with adjacent text, and answering from top-N retrieved chunks. It is effective in open-domain settings, but heterogeneous documents with text and tables expose its central limitations: flattening and fragmentation can destroy tabular structure, lose information, remove the global view, and yield noisy, incomplete, or insufficiently relevant context. Consequently, it may reason over only retrieved portions of a table and produce incorrect results. Existing methodologies are tailored to surface-level table comprehension; task-adaptive approaches seek to address these challenges.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation has demonstrated considerable effectiveness in open-domain question answering. When applied to heterogeneous documents, existing approaches exhibit limitations because table flattening and chunking can disrupt tabular structure, cause information loss, and weaken reasoning.

1

Retrieval-augmented generation commonly linearizes tables, chunks them with adjacent text, and generates answers from the top-N retrieved chunks. The unit shows that this approach can compute over only relevant chunks rather than the full table, producing an incorrect percentage.

5 / 5.1 / 5.1.1 .. 5.3

Retrieval-augmented generation is represented by the standard RAG pipeline used in NaiveRAG, which processes linearized Markdown tables. The unit compares this approach with TableRAG's combination of textual retrieval, context-sensitive decomposition, and program-executed reasoning.

8 / 8.1 .. 8.2

Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant document chunks from a knowledge base and incorporates them into the generation process. It is used to mitigate hallucination and enhance the reliability of generated responses, but straightforward retrieval can yield noisy or incomplete chunks, and heterogeneous contexts remain challenging. Task-adaptive approaches including Self-RAG and RQ-RAG have been developed to address these limitations.

standard RAG in TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text

Songshuo Lu · 2025

Standard RAG retrieves top document chunks for a query, concatenates them, and performs one online prefill to build a KV cache before autoregressive generation. Processing the full context creates significant TTFT latency and resource use. TurboRAG addresses this overhead without changing models or inference systems, reporting up to 9.4× lower TTFT without compromising accuracy.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

RAG systems concatenate and process numerous retrieved document chunks during prefill, leading to significant latency in time-to-first-token. TurboRAG reduces this computation overhead without requiring changes to models or inference systems.

1 / Introduction .. Contributions

Standard RAG computes a single KV cache for the entire concatenated document set online. Compared with standard RAG, TurboRAG achieves up to a 9.4× TTFT reduction and substantially lowers computational resource utilization without compromising accuracy.

3 / Methodology .. 3.4 / The TurboRAG Pipeline

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves top document chunks for a user query and provides their concatenated context to a large language model. Conventional RAG computes a prefill over the concatenated context and query before autoregressive response generation.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text

Songshuo Lu · 2025

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a generation framework and method that couples a dense retriever and a large language model, using external knowledge to ground generation. It is a de-facto solution for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and has documented gains for question answering, code synthesis, and creative writing. Conventionally, it retrieves many document chunks, concatenates them, and prefills them for generation. This design can require substantial online computation, increase time-to-first-token, recompute redundant work, incur quadratic prefill cost, and restrict batch size. Work on accelerating it has reduced retrieved text or decoding cost and reused caches under strict ordering. TurboRAG instead aggregates retrieved document fragments through concatenated pre-computed KV caches. In document-QA and long-context comparisons with Naïve RAG, TurboRAG variants preserve RAG accuracy while reducing inference latency and computation. Its discussion suggests direct query-document interactions can often suffice without expensive cross-attention between fragments.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. TurboRAG: Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Precomputed KV Caches for Chunked Text

Retrieval-augmented generation is identified as the subject that TurboRAG aims to accelerate.

Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems process numerous retrieved document chunks for prefill, which requires substantial online computation and can increase time-to-first-token.

1 / Introduction .. Contributions

Retrieval–Augmented Generation couples a large language model with a dense retriever so that generation can be grounded in external knowledge. Its conventional concatenate-then-prefill design is described as suffering from redundant recomputation, quadratic prefill cost, and restricted batch size.

2 / Related Work

Retrieval-Augmented Generation couples a dense retriever with a large language model to ground generation in external knowledge and is used for knowledge-intensive NLP tasks. Prior acceleration methods reduce retrieved text, reduce decoding cost, or reuse caches under strict ordering.

4 / Experiments .. 4.5 / Batch Scaling

Retrieval-augmented generation is studied by comparing conventional Naïve RAG with TurboRAG variants on document-QA and long-context tasks. The experiments show that TurboRAG can preserve RAG accuracy while reducing inference latency and computation.

5 / Conclusion and Discussion .. Limitations

Retrieval-augmented generation is addressed through a method that directly aggregates retrieved document fragments by concatenating their pre-computed KV caches. The unit suggests that direct query-document interactions can often be sufficient without computationally intensive cross-attention between fragments.

references

The references include foundational and benchmarking work on retrieval-augmented generation, including Lewis et al. (2020), Izacard and Grave (2020), and Chen et al. (2024). They also cover systems and methods for improving retrieval-augmented generation through caching, speculative drafting, context selection, hybrid-model prefix caching, and knowledge fusion, including RAGCache, PiperAG, Speculative RAG, sparse context selection, Marconi, and CacheBlend.

retrieval-augmented generation in VISA: Retrieval Augmented Generation with Visual Source Attribution

Xueguang Ma, Shengyao Zhuang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon, Wenhu Chen, Jimmy Lin · 2025

Retrieval-augmented generation is a solution for hallucinations and outdated internal knowledge in information-seeking: it retrieves relevant documents from an external database and supplies them with a textual query to large language models. It can link generated content to source references, but document-level citations can burden readers and make evidence hard to locate across content-rich documents; passage-level citations need additional engineering. In the defined task, a retrieval component selects candidate documents from a corpus, while a generation component produces an answer, identifies the most relevant document, and locates its supporting content. The Multi-candidate experimental setting gives the generator multiple candidates, including one ground-truth document and hard negatives, and requires evidence selection, answer generation, and a bounding box. With k=20 and m=3, the ground-truth document is replaced 20% of the time to test no-answer detection.

Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation approaches primarily link generated content to document-level references, which makes it difficult to locate evidence within multiple content-rich retrieved documents.

Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation has become a key technique for enhancing reliability in information-seeking processes.

opening

Retrieval-augmented generation with textual source attribution can ask models to generate answers and cite source-document identifiers. Document-level citations can impose a heavy cognitive burden, while passage-level citations require additional engineering to match text chunks to their document sources.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.2

It retrieves relevant documents from an external database and provides them to large language models alongside a question. It is presented as an effective solution to hallucinations and outdated internal knowledge, and it can be combined with source attribution.

3 / 3.1 .. 3.3

In the defined RAG task, a retrieval component selects candidate documents from a corpus, and a generation component produces an answer, identifies the most relevant document, and locates supporting content within it.

opening .. 3.4

The RAG experimental environment gives a generator multiple retrieval candidates and requires it to attribute evidence to the most relevant document. The setup uses one ground-truth document mixed with m−1 hard negatives, sets k=20 and m=3, and randomly replaces the ground-truth document with probability 20% to evaluate no-answer detection.

4 / 4.1 .. 4.2

Retrieval-augmented generation is represented by the Multi-candidate setting, where models receive multiple retrieved documents and must select supporting evidence before generating an answer and bounding box.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus

Soyeong Jeong · 2025

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a strategy and generation framework that combines retrieval with generation. It retrieves query-relevant knowledge from external sources or corpora, supplies it to a foundation model, and generates answers grounded in that content, mitigating inaccurate or outdated parametric knowledge and improving factual accuracy. It has chiefly focused on text, often using sources such as Wikipedia; newer work also considers images or text-image pairs, while videos have largely been overlooked. Advanced approaches can use iterative retrieval-generation cycles. Recent expansion extends the external knowledge source from text and static images to videos, with video retrieval and response generation as components. Case-study results show RAG systems outperform a NAÏVE baseline and suggest videos can provide richer information than textual, text-image, or text-description-based alternatives. VideoRAG incorporates videos rather than only textual representations or assumed relevant videos, while RAG over videos requires evaluation with query, relevant-video, and ground-truth-answer triples.

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant knowledge elements from an external corpus and supplies them to a foundation model to produce an answer. In this unit, the external knowledge source is extended from mainly text and static images to videos.

opening .. Case Study

RAG systems outperform the NAÏVE baseline, supporting the value of external knowledge for factual answer generation. The results indicate that video content can provide richer information than textual, text-image, or text-description-based alternatives.

4 / Retrieval-Augmented Generation .. Large Video Language Models

Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines retrieval and generation to produce answers grounded in external knowledge. Most RAG research has focused on text, leaving comparatively little effort devoted to incorporating images and other modalities.

5

Retrieval-augmented generation is expanded by VideoRAG to incorporate videos as an external knowledge source rather than relying only on textual representations or assuming that relevant videos already exist.

Limitations

RAG over videos requires evaluation using triples consisting of a query, relevant videos, and a ground-truth answer.

RAG in RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems

Robert Friel · 2025-01-16

RAG is a system architecture and architectural pattern for bringing domain-specific knowledge into user-facing chat and dialogue applications powered by Large Language Models. It combines a retriever, which queries relevant documents from an in-domain corpus, with a generator that uses those documents and the user query to produce an informed response. Its central purpose is to ground models in factual information and improve knowledge-intensive NLP tasks, including open-domain question answering. Retrieved documents are generally semantically related to the query, but the records stress that semantic similarity alone does not prove that context is relevant for answering it. RAG is increasingly used in real-world applications and develops through iterative improvement of RAG models. Evaluation is a major concern: it examines retrieved context, generated answers, hallucinations, attribution, adherence, relevance, utilization, completeness, and system-level correctness. RAGTruth provides a hallucination corpus; RAGAs and ARES evaluate it; CRAG and Chinese domain-specific DomainRAG are benchmarks; and validation data are sampled from KILT, including Natural Questions, HotpotQA, FEVER, and Wizards of Wikipedia. RAGBench standardizes 12 component datasets into the RAG format, varying document count, context length, source domain, and response-generation model to represent real-world scenarios. Its simulated systems retrieve context and generate responses, using TF-IDF or FAISS retrieval, different context and prompt settings, and GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 or GPT-4o. The work culminates in a goal of more precise, actionable evaluation for real-world RAG systems.

Narrative, section by section

11 sections; each heading opens the text

RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems

Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems are the subject of the explainable benchmark introduced in this unit.

Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation has become a standard architectural pattern for incorporating domain-specific knowledge into user-facing chat applications powered by Large Language Models.

Introduction

Retriever-Augmented Generation combines a retriever that queries relevant documents from an in-domain corpus with a generator model that uses those documents and the original user query to produce an informed response. It helps ground Large Language Models in factual information and improves knowledge-intensive task performance.

Related Work .. Finetuned RAG evaluation models

Retrieval-augmented generation is evaluated through approaches that examine retrieved context, generated answers, hallucinations, attribution, and system-level correctness.

RAGBench Construction / Component Datasets .. Data Splits

Retrieval-augmented generation is the format into which the 12 component datasets are standardized. RAGBench varies context-document count, context length, source domain, and response-generation model to represent different real-world RAG scenarios.

RAG Case Study .. Estimating Context Relevance is Difficult

RAG is evaluated through simulated systems that retrieve context documents and generate responses for questions. The unit emphasizes that semantic similarity between a query and retrieved context does not by itself establish that the context is relevant to answering the question.

Conclusion

The paper aims to advance retrieval-augmented generation by enabling more precise and actionable evaluation of its systems in real-world applications.

references

Retrieval-augmented generation is addressed through foundational work, surveys, domain-adaptation studies, and benchmarks such as RAGAs, ARES, CRAG, DomainRAG, and RAGTruth. The references examine evaluation, attribution, hallucination detection, and the use of retrieved information in knowledge-intensive and domain-specific question answering.

RAGBench Dataset Details .. ExpertQA [25]

RAG is the task format used to reframe many of the component datasets in RAGBench. The benchmark forms examples from questions and retrieved or supplied context documents, then generally generates responses with an LLM.

Annotation Alignment with Human Judgements / Adherence Alignment with DelucionQA .. Rank-based Alignment for Adherence and Relevance

The RAG validation data are sampled from KILT and include Natural Questions, HotpotQA, FEVER, and Wizards of Wikipedia. The analysis examines whether annotations of context relevance and answer adherence recover the ground-truth ranking of systems with different quality levels.

DeBERTa model training

RAG is evaluated using TF-IDF and FAISS retrievers, k values of 2 and 4, prompt versions of no context, short, long, and long + CoT, and GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 or GPT-4o. The evaluation measures average relevance, average utilization, average completeness, and the percentage of hallucinated responses.

RAG in RAGBench: Explainable Benchmark for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems

Robert Friel · 2025-01-16

RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, is a system/technology with two components: a document retriever and a downstream Large Language Models response-generation component. It queries a domain-specific corpus for context relevant to an input query, then generates a response from the query and retrieved context. It can boost knowledge-intensive tasks through additional context, but production settings can include hallucinations. Its design varies by retriever, retrieved-document number, generation model, context format and length, and generation prompt, so application-specific optimization is complex and costly and requires balancing accuracy and efficiency. Evaluation is challenging because unified criteria and annotated datasets are lacking. TRACe evaluates relevance, utilization, adherence, and completeness: retrievers should return necessary information without superfluous data, while generators should rely strictly on context. In simulated systems, retriever configuration affects relevance, and LLM and prompt choices affect utilization, hallucinations, and completeness. Benchmarks and methodologies provide insights into strengths and weaknesses for iterative improvement.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

RAG systems use a document retriever to query a domain-specific corpus for context relevant to an input query, and an LLM to generate a response from the query and context. Their comprehensive evaluation remains challenging because unified evaluation criteria and annotated datasets are lacking.

Introduction

RAG systems comprise a retriever component and a downstream LLM generator model. Their design involves multiple choices of retriever and generator models and other variable parameters, making application-specific optimization complex and costly.

Related Work .. Finetuned RAG evaluation models

RAG systems are evaluated across multiple components and dimensions, including retriever relevance, response adherence, and response completeness. Their workflow can vary by context format and length, retriever model, number of retrieved documents, and generation model.

TRACe Evaluation Framework .. Adherence

RAG is evaluated as a system whose retriever should return the necessary information without superfluous data and whose response generator should base its output strictly on the provided context.

RAGBench Statistics .. Alignment with Human Judgements

The reported RAG system analysis examines how retriever choice and configuration affect context Relevance, and how LLM and prompt choices affect context Utilization, hallucinations, and Completeness. In the example, a dense retriever with k=2 produces the highest average context Relevance, while a detailed chain-of-thought prompt reduces hallucinations and increases Utilization and Completeness.

RAG Case Study .. Estimating Context Relevance is Difficult

The RAG systems are simulated by varying the retriever, number of retrieved documents, generation model, and generation prompt template. Responses from 32 systems are evaluated using the TRACe metrics.

Conclusion

RAG systems are evaluated using the standardized TRACe framework across utilization, relevance, adherence, and completeness. The proposed benchmarks and methodologies are intended to provide actionable insights into their strengths and weaknesses and support iterative improvement.

RAG architecture in SafetyRAG: Towards Safe Large Language Model-Based Application through Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Sihem Omri, Manel Abdelkader, and Mohamed Hamdi · 2025-02-17

RAG architecture is the underlying architecture for SafetyRAG, an LLM-based medical-assistant approach that supplies domain-specific context from a knowledge base. A user prompt is encoded, used to retrieve relevant knowledge, and that information is provided as context for generation. When a harmful prompt is encountered, it supplies explicit information about it to promote safe behavior. Across the study, it improves awareness of unsafe behaviors through appropriate safety facts and is described as easy to implement across LLM-based applications without additional costs versus existing alternatives.

The RAG architecture is used by SafetyRAG to provide an LLM with explicit information about a harmful prompt when it is encountered. This information is intended to enhance the LLM's safe behavior.

The RAG architecture provides the basis for SafetyRAG. In this framework, a user prompt is encoded, used to retrieve relevant information from a knowledge database, and supplied as context for generation.

The RAG architecture improves models' awareness of unsafe behaviors by retrieving and providing appropriate safety facts. The study describes this approach as easy to implement across various LLM-based applications and as not incurring additional costs compared with existing alternatives.

Retrieval Augmented Generation in Ragas: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation

Shahul Es, Jithin James, Luis Espinosa-Anke, Steven Schockaert · 2025-04-28

Retrieval Augmented Generation is a standard solution to limitations of language models. It consists of a retrieval module and an LLM-based generation module: it retrieves relevant passages from a reference textual database or corpus, then feeds them with the original question to a language model to generate an answer. It provides knowledge to large language models, creates a natural language layer between users and textual databases, and reduces hallucination risk. Its performance depends on the retrieval model, corpus, language model, and prompt formulation. Because systems usually lack human-annotated datasets and reference answers, they need automated, reference-free evaluation, including assessment of faithfulness, retrieved-passage usefulness, and often perplexity on a reference corpus.

RAG systems consist of a retrieval module and an LLM-based generation module. They provide large language models with knowledge from a reference textual database, allowing them to act as a natural language layer between users and textual databases while reducing the risk of hallucinations.

Retrieval Augmented Generation addresses limitations of Language Models by retrieving relevant passages from a corpus and providing them to the model along with the original question. Its performance depends on factors including the retrieval model, corpus, Language Model, and prompt formulation.

2 .. Faithfulness

Retrieval augmented generation systems first retrieve context for a question and then use that context to generate an answer. The unit considers methods for estimating their correctness and the usefulness of their retrieved passages without human-annotated datasets or reference answers.

Conclusions

RAG systems are identified as needing automated reference-free evaluation.

RAG in Knowledge Graph-Guided Retrieval Augmented Generation

Xiangrong Zhu · 2025-04-29/2025-05-04

RAG is a promising technology and generation approach for mitigating hallucinations in large language model responses caused by missing or outdated knowledge. It processes provided or candidate documents by splitting them into sentence- and paragraph-based chunks of predefined size, encoding and indexing chunks with an embedding model, retrieving relevant chunks for a query, and integrating them into prompts for generation. Existing semantic-based retrieval can return isolated, homogeneous, or redundant chunks without representing relationships among information. KG2RAG extends this document-processing approach with knowledge-graph-based retrieval and organization and is reported to improve response and retrieval quality. Retrieval-augmented generation methods improve over an LLM-only approach on original and shuffled HotpotQA datasets. RAG remains a systematic engineering framework that can be refined through query rewriting, retrieval optimization, multi-turn dialogue, and other approaches.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation has emerged as a promising technology for addressing hallucination issues in responses generated by large language models. Existing studies primarily use semantic-based approaches to retrieve isolated relevant chunks.

1

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant knowledge from provided documents and incorporates it into language-model prompts. Existing approaches may retrieve homogeneous or redundant chunks and concatenate them without representing relationships among the information.

2 / 2.1 .. 2.3

RAG is described as a setting in which documents are split into chunks and retrieved chunks are integrated into prompts for LLMs. KG2RAG follows this document-processing approach while adding knowledge-graph-based retrieval and organization.

3 / 3.1 .. 3.3

Retrieval-augmented generation methods substantially improve over the LLM-only approach on both the original and shuffled HotpotQA datasets. The experiments assess these methods through both the quality of generated responses and the quality of retrieved chunks and organized context.

4

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant chunks from candidate documents to assist large language model generation and address hallucinations caused by missing or outdated knowledge. Typical systems segment documents into chunks, encode and index them, and retrieve them for use with queries.

5

Retrieval-augmented generation is enhanced by KG2RAG through the integration of knowledge graphs. KG2RAG is reported to outperform existing retrieval-augmented generation approaches in both response quality and retrieval quality.

Limitations

Retrieval-augmented generation is a systematic engineering framework that can be refined through query rewriting, retrieval optimization, multi-turn dialogue, and other approaches.

RAG in RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models

Bang An · 2025-04-29/2025-05-04

RAG is a framework and model setting in which relevant documents are identified from a corpus and supplied as context for large language models (LLMs), which synthesize that material into responses. It is widely used, with popular strategies using documents alone or documents plus model knowledge. Its central importance is that grounding responses in source documents can reduce hallucinations and facilitate attributed generation, yet it can also change safety profiles: most LLMs in RAG settings show more unsafe responses than in non-RAG settings, even when both models and retrieved documents are safe. RAG can amplify existing unsafe behavior, introduce vulnerabilities across nearly every safety category, and become less safe with additional context; even one relevant document can alter safety behavior. In the evaluated system, BM25 retrieves five paragraph-level documents from an English Wikipedia corpus, under document-only and document-plus-knowledge settings. RAG-specific jailbreaking prompts are more effective than transferred prompts, though altering retrieval reduces their success. These vulnerabilities create distinct challenges for safety fine-tuning, red-teaming, and dynamic corpora.

Narrative, section by section

8 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

RAG can make models less safe and change their safety profile. The unit finds that even combinations of safe models and safe documents can produce unsafe generations.

Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation identifies relevant documents from a corpus and provides them to a large language model to support a response. The unit finds that RAG can make relatively safe models unsafe, even when the retrieved documents are safe.

Definitions

RAG uses retrieved documents as context for LLM generation. Most LLMs in the RAG setting exhibit a significantly higher percentage of unsafe responses than in the non-RAG setting.

RQ1: Are RAG-based LLMs safer than

The evaluated RAG system uses BM25 to retrieve five paragraph-level documents from an English Wikipedia corpus containing 20,464,398 documents. It is tested in settings that use retrieved documents alone or together with the model’s own knowledge.

RQ2: What makes RAG-based LLMs .. Factor 3: An LLM’s Capability on RAG

Retrieval-augmented generation can amplify existing unsafe behaviors and introduce new vulnerabilities. Even one relevant document can change a model's safety behavior, while adding more context generally increases unsafe responses.

RQ3: Are red-teaming methods .. Applying Jailbreaking Methods to RAG

RAG-based models can become unsafe even when the underlying models are safe. Jailbreaking prompts trained directly for RAG achieve higher effectiveness than prompts transferred from non-RAG settings, but their success declines when the prompts alter retrieval.

Discussions on Future Directions

RAG involves LLMs synthesizing information from retrieved documents. Its setting creates distinct challenges for safety fine-tuning, red-teaming, and the use of dynamic corpora.

Ethics Statement

The RAG setting is identified as an environment in which people have overlooked vulnerabilities of LLMs.

RAG LLMs in RAG LLMs are Not Safer: A Safety Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models

Bang An · 2025-04-29/2025-05-04

RAG LLMs are language models that synthesize retrieved documents and therefore have safety requirements distinct from non-RAG models. Research has mainly examined corpus poisoning, alongside corpus leakage, retriever robustness to noise, and resilience to document perturbations, including settings with carefully controlled corpora. In evaluation, they are not safer than non-RAG counterparts: eight of eleven models show markedly different safety behavior, and several produce substantially more unsafe responses. Their safety is shaped by inherent LLM safety, retrieved-document safety, and capability on RAG tasks; unsafe outputs can occur even with safe retrieved documents. They introduce new unsafe outputs in addition to inherited vulnerabilities, often appearing more vulnerable, motivating dedicated RAG safety research.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Related Work

Research on RAG LLM safety mainly focuses on corpus poisoning, while also addressing corpus leakage, retriever robustness to noise, and resilience to document perturbations. The unit considers RAG LLMs in scenarios where the corpus is carefully controlled.

RQ1: Are RAG-based LLMs safer than

RAG-based LLMs are not safer than their non-RAG counterparts in this evaluation. Eight of eleven models show markedly different safety behavior under RAG, with large increases in unsafe responses for several models.

RQ2: What makes RAG-based LLMs .. Factor 3: An LLM’s Capability on RAG

RAG-based LLMs are generally less safe than their non-RAG counterparts, and their safety is shaped by inherent model safety, retrieved-document safety, and capability on RAG tasks. They can produce unsafe responses even when retrieved documents are safe.

Discussions on Future Directions

RAG-based LLMs exhibit different and often more vulnerable safety behaviors. They synthesize information from retrieved documents, creating safety requirements distinct from those of non-RAG models.

retrieval-augmented generation in Enhancing treatment decision-making for low back pain: a novel framework integrating large language models with retrieval-augmented generation technology

Rong Chen, Siyun Zhang, Yiyi Zheng, Qiuhua Yu and Chuhuai Wang · 2025-05-14

Retrieval-augmented generation is a technology and generative AI framework that combines information retrieval, text generation, large language models, and external knowledge bases. In the proposed clinical decision-support framework, it supports personalized treatment decision-making for chronic low back pain. It matters because it expands models beyond training-data limitations, addressing outdated information and inaccurate facts while improving professionalism, accuracy, interpretability, and grounding in validated guidelines. The framework builds a vector knowledge base from medical literature and guidelines from 2021–2025, extracts characteristic keywords from clinical scenarios, retrieves relevant knowledge through cosine similarity, and supplies it to prompting. Its dynamic retrieval matches scenarios to current evidence and is intended to reduce hallucination risk.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. Enhancing treatment decision-making for low back pain: a novel framework integrating large language models with retrieva

Retrieval-augmented generation technology was combined with large language models to support clinical decision-making and personalized treatment for chronic low back pain.

1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation combines information retrieval with text generation by retrieving relevant material from external knowledge bases and using it to generate answers. In this study, it is used to compensate for language model knowledge limitations and improve the professionalism, accuracy, and interpretability of medical decision-making.

2 Materials and methods / 2.1 Framework .. 2.4 LtM prompting

Retrieval-augmented generation combines large language models with external knowledge bases to address limitations involving outdated information and inaccurate facts. In this study, it retrieves relevant CLBP knowledge using extracted characteristic keywords and cosine similarity before the information is supplied to the prompting stage.

5 Discussion

Retrieval-augmented generation is implemented through a dynamic knowledge retrieval mechanism that matches clinical scenarios with current domain-specific evidence. This mechanism is described as reducing hallucination risk and helping recommendations remain grounded in validated clinical guidelines.

retrieval augmented generation (RAG) in Retrieval augmented generation for large language models in healthcare: A systematic review

Lameck Mbangula Amugongo · 2025-06-11

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) is a method, approach, and framework for grounding Large Language Model responses by exposing models to external knowledge sources. It combines information retrieval with in-context learning, supplying relevant, up-to-date, and user-specific information that may not be in pre-trained knowledge, without computationally expensive retraining or fine-tuning. Its central purpose is to improve factuality, reduce hallucinations, enhance transparency of completion sources, and strengthen response accuracy, reliability, interpretability, and specialized medical reasoning. In medical question answering, it addresses both missing current medical information and the tendency of models to make things up. RAG unfolds through three core parts: a user prompt, retrieval of relevant external context, and generation of an output using both the prompt and retrieved context. The reviewed work considers what information to retrieve, when to retrieve it, and how to use it. Its development is grouped into three paradigms: Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG; Modular RAG has more complex pre-retrieval and post-retrieval processing. Evaluation commonly considers the prompt, retrieval, and generated output, often assessing the retriever and generator separately, though comprehensive evaluation remains unsettled.

Narrative, section by section

7 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Retrieval augmented generation (RAG) addresses limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) by exposing them to external knowledge sources and grounding their responses. The review examines Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG approaches in healthcare, focusing on retrieval, augmentation, and generation.

Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation combines LLMs with relevant information retrieved from external knowledge sources before generating an answer. In healthcare, it is intended to reduce hallucinations, improve transparency, and incorporate current clinical data and reliable medical sources.

Methods .. Exclusion criteria

RAG is described as a way to provide LLMs with up-to-date and user-specific information that is not part of their pre-trained knowledge, thereby grounding the LLM. The review identifies and evaluates RAG-based methods applied in the medical domain.

Results / Included studies .. Datasets

Retrieval-augmented generation is used to ground medical language-model responses with external knowledge. The reviewed approaches address what information to retrieve, when to retrieve it, and how to use it.

RAG overview .. Advanced RAG

Retrieval-augmented generation grounds large language models in external knowledge to improve factuality, reduce hallucination, and provide information that may be more current than the models’ training data. It combines information retrieval with in-context learning without requiring computationally expensive retraining or fine-tuning.

Modular RAG

Retrieval-augmented generation is presented as a framework used across healthcare applications to improve retrieval, response accuracy, reliability, interpretability, and specialized medical reasoning. The reviewed implementations are grouped into Naive, Advanced, and Modular RAG, with Modular RAG characterized by more complex pre-retrieval and post-retrieval processing.

Evaluation metrics and frameworks

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system is evaluated through the user prompt, retrieval of relevant context, and generation of an output using the prompt and retrieved context. Its evaluation commonly separates the retriever and generator, although comprehensive evaluation remains unsettled.

RAG pipelines in Retrieval augmented generation for large language models in healthcare: A systematic review

Lameck Mbangula Amugongo · 2025-06-11

RAG pipelines are a method and healthcare approach for grounding large language models with knowledge retrieved from external sources. They can improve performance, reduce hallucination, and constrain incorrect output, while still being affected by hallucination when retrieval is irrelevant or generation is unpredictable. They do not ensure correctness or eliminate bias, and retrieval can expose information from pre-training, fine-tuning, or retrieval datasets. In healthcare, their implementation involves datasets, language models, embedding models, retrieval methods, pre-retrieval strategies, and prompting techniques. The approach develops through naive, advanced, and modular RAG paradigms. Many studies optimize retrieval and generation, but conventional single-round retrieval may not handle complex medical queries requiring multi-hop reasoning. Unresolved issues include retrieval quality, context length, evaluation standardization, privacy, safety, noise, source factuality, information integration, and ethical considerations. RAG pipelines can integrate dynamic data, standards, and individual healthcare scenarios to ground and customize domain knowledge, with potential applications in drug development, disease prediction, and personalised care management.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Ethical considerations

Retrieval augmented generation grounds LLM responses in knowledge retrieved from external sources and can improve performance, reduce hallucinations, and constrain incorrect output. However, it does not guarantee correctness, eliminate bias, or prevent exposure of information from pre-training, fine-tuning, or retrieval datasets.

Data analysis

The unit reviews how retrieval-augmented generation is implemented in healthcare, including its datasets, language models, embedding models, retrieval methods, pre-retrieval strategies, and prompting techniques.

Discussion

Retrieval-augmented generation is reviewed as a healthcare approach organized into naive, advanced, and modular paradigms. The unit reports that many studies optimize retrieval and generation, but that conventional single-round retrieval may be inadequate for complex medical queries requiring multi-hop reasoning. It also highlights unresolved problems involving retrieval quality, hallucination, context length, evaluation standardization, privacy, and safety.

Conclusion

RAG is presented as a method for grounding and customizing LLM domain knowledge in healthcare by integrating dynamic data, standards, and individual scenarios. It has potential applications in drug development, disease prediction, and personalized care management, but effective implementation requires addressing information integration, noise, source factuality, and ethical considerations.

Author contributions

Retrieval augmented generation appears in the title as the subject of a review concerning large language models in healthcare.

Naive RAG in Question Decomposition for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Paul J. L. Ammann · 2025-07-28/2025-07-29

Naive RAG is a standard retrieval-augmented generation approach and base setup for grounding LLMs in external sources. At inference time, it encodes a user question once, uses single-query dense retrieval to select the top-k semantically relevant passages, and conditions a language model on the question and retrieved evidence. It is particularly effective for question answering, but depends heavily on retrieval quality: irrelevant documents can degrade output. As a naive baseline, it assumes the top-ranked passages contain all necessary evidence, treats questions as single-hop, and ignores multi-step reasoning and dependencies across documents. It is the fastest evaluated system, taking 0.03 seconds per query, but has lower retrieval quality and HotpotQA answer performance than QD+RR; its supporting-fact F1, precision, and recall are 18.4, 12.0, and 42.8.

Narrative, section by section

5 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves passages semantically related to a question and conditions the model on that evidence. The proposed pipeline enhances RAG for multi-hop questions through question decomposition and reranking.

Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation addresses knowledge gaps in large language models by retrieving external information at inference time. Its performance depends heavily on retrieval quality, and irrelevant documents can mislead the model and degrade its output.

RAG with Question Decomposition .. QD Module / Reranker Module

RAG normally encodes the user query once, retrieves the top-k relevant passages, and provides them with the query to a language model. The proposed pipeline augments this framework with question decomposition and reranking.

Experiments / Datasets .. HotpotQA

Naive RAG embeds a single query and retrieves the top-k most relevant passages from the corpus using dense retrieval. It serves as the base configuration for comparison.

opening .. Efficiency

Naive RAG is the fastest evaluated system at 0.03 seconds per query. It provides lower retrieval quality than QD+RR and lower HotpotQA answer performance than QD+RR, while its supporting-fact metrics are 18.4 F1, 12.0 precision, and 42.8 recall.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Question Decomposition for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Paul J. L. Ammann · 2025-07-28/2025-07-29

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a framework, following Lewis et al. (2020), that combines a retriever and a generative language model. At inference time, it grounds answers to natural-language queries in documents retrieved from a large corpus, giving large language models access to external information for up-to-date or specialized knowledge. It supports knowledge-intensive, open-domain, complex, and multi-hop question answering, though results depend heavily on retrieval quality. For complex questions, question decomposition and cross-encoder reranking together improve retrieval and answer correctness without extra training or domain-specific tuning.

3 sections; each heading opens the text

Methodology .. Generation.

The retrieval-augmented generation framework combines a retriever with a generative language model to answer a natural language query by grounding the response in documents retrieved from a large corpus.

Related Work / RAG augments LLMs with access to

Retrieval-Augmented Generation augments large language models with access to external information at inference time, addressing limitations involving up-to-date or specialized knowledge. It has shown promise for knowledge-intensive tasks including open-domain and multi-hop question answering, but its performance depends heavily on retrieval quality.

Reranking for Precision Retrieval. / Complementary Approaches. / Conclusion .. Future work. Employing QD only when a query

The unit evaluates question decomposition and cross-encoder reranking within retrieval-augmented generation for complex and multi-hop question answering. Their combination improves retrieval and answer correctness without extra training or domain-specific tuning.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation in A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models

Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Zheng Yuan, Huachi Zhou, Zijin Hong, Hao Chen, Yilin Xiao, Chuang Zhou, Junnan Dong, Yi Chang, Xiao Huang · 2025-09-29

Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a framework and approach for customizing large language models for specific or professional fields without changing their architecture or parameters. It integrates pre-constructed external knowledge bases, enabling real-time access to domain-specific expertise during inference. Its traditional pipeline unfolds through knowledge preparation, retrieval of relevant external information, and integration of that information to prompt generation. By grounding responses in retrieved knowledge, it aims to make content more substantiated and accurate and to reduce hallucinations and inconsistencies. Its basic pipeline nevertheless faces challenges in complex query understanding, distributed knowledge integration, context limits, and efficiency.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract—Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated

Retrieval-Augmented Generation customizes large language models for professional fields by integrating external knowledge bases and enabling real-time access to domain-specific expertise during inference.

I. INTRODUCTION

Retrieval-augmented generation customizes large language models by supplying external knowledge from text corpora without modifying model parameters or architecture. Its basic pipeline includes knowledge preparation, retrieval, and integration, but it faces challenges in complex query understanding, distributed knowledge integration, context limits, and efficiency.

III. WHAT IS GRAPHRAG / A. Traditional RAG Pipeline .. D. Traditional RAG vs GraphRAG

Retrieval-augmented generation retrieves relevant information from external knowledge bases and uses it to guide large language model generation. It is intended to produce more substantiated and accurate content while reducing hallucinations and inconsistencies.

D. Traditional RAG Pipeline

RAG retrieves relevant information from external knowledge bases and uses it to prompt large language models. It can make generated content more substantiated and accurate while minimizing hallucinations and inconsistencies.

RAG in A Survey of Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Customized Large Language Models

Qinggang Zhang, Shengyuan Chen, Yuanchen Bei, Zheng Yuan, Huachi Zhou, Zijin Hong, Hao Chen, Yilin Xiao, Chuang Zhou, Junnan Dong, Yi Chang, Xiao Huang · 2025-09-29

RAG is a promising solution that enhances LLMs’ domain-specific capabilities by integrating external knowledge bases. Traditional RAG is based on flat text retrieval: it organizes document collections into text chunks in vector databases and retrieves chunks through semantic similarity, KNN, TF-IDF, or BM25. Its core components are knowledge organization, knowledge retrieval, and knowledge integration. Traditional systems struggle with structured knowledge, complex professional and multi-hop queries, distributed sources, long-distance dependencies, excessive retrieved content, large-scale unstructured sources, and efficiency and contextual coherence. These limitations motivate GraphRAG, particularly for structured knowledge and more effective integration across sources.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract—Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated

Traditional RAG systems face challenges in understanding complex professional queries, integrating knowledge across distributed sources, and maintaining efficiency at scale.

II. OVERVIEW

Retrieval-augmented generation is represented through traditional RAG systems, whose limitations in handling structured knowledge motivate the introduction of GraphRAG.

III. WHAT IS GRAPHRAG / A. Traditional RAG Pipeline .. D. Traditional RAG vs GraphRAG

Traditional RAG organizes knowledge as text chunks in vector databases and commonly retrieves content using semantic similarity, KNN, TF-IDF, or BM25. It can struggle with complex multi-hop queries, distributed domain knowledge, excessive retrieved content, long-distance dependencies, and large-scale unstructured sources.

VII. CONCLUSION

RAG enhances LLMs' domain-specific capabilities by integrating external knowledge bases. Traditional RAG systems face difficulties efficiently processing extensive document collections, combining knowledge from multiple sources, and maintaining contextual coherence during retrieval and generation.

retrieval-augmented generation in MEGA-RAG: a retrieval-augmented generation framework with multi-evidence guided answer refinement for mitigating hallucinations of LLMs in public health

Shan Xu, Zhaokun Yan, Chengxiao Dai and Fan Wu · 2025-10-08

Retrieval-augmented generation is a framework approach that combines a large language model with external knowledge to improve responses to public health queries and partially mitigate hallucinations. It can be enhanced with knowledge graphs and external knowledge bases to improve retrieval, reasoning, and healthcare applications. In the experimental setting, it forms both a standard LLM + RAG baseline and the basis for MEGA-RAG. Standard RAG restricts candidate retrieval to external documents; MEGA-RAG extends it through multi-source evidence retrieval, dense retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking, weighted entailment scoring, and multi-evidence guided answer refinement.

LLM + RAG in MEGA-RAG: a retrieval-augmented generation framework with multi-evidence guided answer refinement for mitigating hallucinations of LLMs in public health

Shan Xu, Zhaokun Yan, Chengxiao Dai and Fan Wu · 2025-10-08

LLM + RAG is a standard retrieval-augmented generation approach that combines a large language model with retrieved external evidence for contextual grounding. It uses PubMed as its external knowledge source and LLaMA3-70B as its implementation model. In evaluation, it achieves 0.6281 accuracy and a 0.6739 F1-score, with 121 false positives and 210 false negatives. In the silver ion water case, it reduces outright fabrication but still offers speculative antiviral mechanisms without rigorous support.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

3 Methods / 3.1 MEGA-RAG framework .. 3.6 Final answer fusion module

Standard RAG is described as retrieving external documents to provide contextual grounding for a large language model. Compared with standard RAG, MEGA-RAG uses multiple retrieval sources, multiple candidate answers, consistency evaluation, and self-clarification.

4 Experiment / 4.1 Datasets .. 4.3 Experimental setting

LLM + RAG combines a large language model with retrieval-augmented generation and external knowledge from the PubMed database. It achieves an accuracy of 0.6281 and an F1-score of 0.6739, and it is implemented using LLaMA3-70B.

5 Results .. 5.3 Evaluating hallucinations in diﬀerent

LLM + RAG is evaluated as a standard RAG approach and obtains an F1 Score of 0.6739. Its confusion matrix contains 121 false positives and 210 false negatives, and in the silver ion water case it reduces outright fabrication but still presents speculative antiviral mechanisms lacking rigorous support.

RAG in OG-RAG: Ontology-grounded retrieval-augmented generation for large language models

Kartik Sharma · 2025-11-04/2025-11-09

RAG is a retrieval-augmented generation model and traditional retrieval-based method that uses domain-agnostic embeddings and maximum inner product search to retrieve query-relevant, contiguous chunks from domain-specific documents for answering. It improves large language model performance, but its central limitation is that it does not account for structured domain knowledge and therefore misses deep conceptual relationships and nuanced facts, producing suboptimal context. As a baseline, it has low Context Recall and Context Entity Recall across Soybean, Wheat, and News, and generally lower context quality, answer quality, and human-attributed support than OG-RAG. It nonetheless has the lowest or near-lowest preprocessing and query times. OG-RAG extends the retrieval-augmented generation framework with ontology-grounded retrieval and greater control over context.

Narrative, section by section

6 sections; each heading opens the text

Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods, including RAG, improve large language model performance but fail to account for structured domain knowledge, which leads to suboptimal context generation.

Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation uses domain-agnostic embeddings to retrieve query-relevant information from domain-specific documents for answering. Existing retrieval-based approaches are described as promising but limited in capturing deep conceptual relationships and nuanced facts.

Related Work

Retrieval augmented generation is identified as a traditional retrieval approach. Graph-based methods are presented as extensions that organize and retrieve contextually relevant information.

Experimental Setup

RAG is a retrieval-based baseline that retrieves relevant contiguous document chunks using maximum inner product search. Its Context Recall and Context Entity Recall are 0.22 and 0.08 for Soybean, 0.14 and 0.04 for Wheat, and 0.01 and 0.01 for News.

Experiments / Query answering .. Ontology sensitivity

RAG serves as a baseline retrieval method for query answering, human context attribution, and factual deduction. It generally produces lower context quality, answer quality, and human-attributed support than OG-RAG, although it has the lowest or near-lowest preprocessing and query times.

Conclusion

Retrieval-augmented generation is the framework in which OG-RAG performs ontology-grounded retrieval. OG-RAG provides greater flexibility and control over how context is retrieved and utilized.

retrieval-augmented generation in An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance

Fidelis Fidelis Alu and Sunkanmi Oluwadare · 2026-02-04

Retrieval-augmented generation is a technology and method for citation-assisted generation: it searches curated medical literature and databases, processes retrieved texts with patient data, and synthesizes recommendations or summaries. Its central purpose is source verification, linking each generated claim to identifiable clinical guidelines, peer-reviewed sources, or specific repository documents. In the proposed framework, it is constrained to verified retrieved sources and records retrieval and decision pathways through audit logging. Citation fidelity remains a feasibility challenge.

Narrative, section by section

4 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation

Retrieval-augmented generation is integrated into the framework to connect generated clinical recommendations with identifiable clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources.

1 Introduction

Retrieval-augmented generation is identified as an approach to be integrated with data provenance in the proposed framework. The design has a system search curated medical literature and databases before an AI module synthesizes an answer.

2 Background and related work

Retrieval-augmented generation systems commonly present evidence-based documents alongside AI-generated summaries. The unit distinguishes these citation-assisted approaches from the proposed framework, which constrains reasoning to verified retrieved sources and records the retrieval and decision pathway.

3 Methods (framework design) .. 3.3.4 Step 4: Forensic audit logging

Retrieval-augmented generation is used to process retrieved medical texts together with patient data and generate recommendations. The generated output is designed to link each claim to specific documents in the curated repository.

RAG architectures in An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation with data provenance

Fidelis Fidelis Alu and Sunkanmi Oluwadare · 2026-02-04

RAG architectures are systems for clinical AI decision support that map and disambiguate clinical language, retrieve evidence, and generate patient-specific recommendations linked to clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Their central challenge is citation fidelity: generated citations can be unsupported or misattributed. The framework addresses this risk through confidence scoring, ensemble retrieval, post-hoc verification, forensic audit logging, and future citation-verification and mitigation modules.

Narrative, section by section

3 sections; each heading opens the text

front matter .. An auditable and source-verified framework for clinical AI decision support: integrating retrieval-augmented generation

The retrieval-augmented reasoning engine links generated recommendations to identifiable clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Citation fidelity within this type of architecture is identified as a feasibility challenge.

3 Methods (framework design) .. 3.3.4 Step 4: Forensic audit logging

The Retrieval and Reasoning Engine maps clinical language to normalized concepts, retrieves relevant evidence, and uses a retrieval-augmented generation architecture to produce cited recommendations. It incorporates confidence scoring, ensemble retrieval, and post-hoc verification to reduce unsupported or misattributed citations.

4 Discussion .. 4.2 Bias mitigation and evidence equity

RAG architectures are identified as having limitations, particularly the risk of citation misattribution. Future implementations will require mitigation strategies and citation-verification modules.
